title: Lesson 30: Keeping the Skill Sharp: Staying Current as Tools Change
description: Durable habits versus perishable tool details, what a drifting routine really signals, and the small repair that restores it.

questions.question: A menu has moved and a model has been renamed. Which part of your skill does that affect?
options: The durable habits of briefing, checking, and deciding
The perishable details that describe one specific tool
Both equally, so the whole skill has to be rebuilt
Neither, because tool details never matter to the work
questions.explanation: Button names, menu positions, and current model names belong to the tool and change without warning. The habits of briefing, reviewing, and checking carry across tools.

questions.question: A weekly routine has quietly stopped doing its job, though the writing still reads well. What is the most likely cause?
options: The person forgot the underlying skill
The output is fine and the complaint is imaginary
An assumption about the tool's behavior quietly changed
The task itself is no longer worth doing
questions.explanation: The habit stayed intact while a default it relied on moved. The failure shows up as output that looks polished but no longer serves its purpose.

questions.question: What is the right response when a recurring routine drifts?
options: Rewrite the whole workflow from scratch
Stop using the tool for that task
Wait for a later release to restore the old behavior
State the assumption explicitly in the prompt and retest
questions.explanation: The skill was never the problem, so the repair is small: make the implicit assumption explicit and run the routine again on real work.
